lens: The evidence pool lacks directly provided facts, making it impossible to construct a thesis grounded in citable primary data; any research direction would rely on speculative extrapolation from unverified hints, which is unpublishable without foundational evidence.
known_to_ignore: Epigenetic clocks show strong correlation with chronological age (r > 0.8)
Proteomic age clocks predict chronological age with high accuracy (Pearson r ~0.94)
Epigenetic age acceleration is associated with health outcomes in older adults
tensions: GrimAgeAA associates with 8/9 health outcomes while PhenoAgeAA associates with only 4/9, suggesting differential sensitivity across clocks
Proteomic age clock accuracy is validated in Chinese and Finnish biobanks but not tested in ethnically diverse cohorts, creating a generalizability gap
Epigenetic aging acceleration linked to gravidity (n=331) may conflict with null findings in smaller studies, indicating population-specific effects
gaps: Epigenetic age acceleration in COVID-19 survivors beyond 6 months post-diagnosis, stratified by severity and comorbidities
Proteomic clock validation in African or Latin American biobanks to assess cross-ethnic robustness
Interaction between parity and epigenetic aging in women with obesity (BMI >30), as current data only cover BMI 25-30 subgroups
reviewer_objections: No primary evidence facts are provided to support any thesis, rendering the analysis speculative and non-replicable
Reliance on untagged hints violates citation standards and undermines scholarly rigor
Proposed gaps lack empirical basis from existing studies, risking publication of anecdotal insights
next_extractions: Epigenetic age acceleration in longitudinal COVID-19 cohorts with biomarker data (e.g., IL-6, CRP)
Proteomic aging clock performance in biobanks from underrepresented regions (e.g., Africa, South America)
Dose-response relationship between gravidity (number of pregnancies) and epigenetic aging across ethnicities with matched controls
